utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-13a-PT, Prosecutor v Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: May we have the appearances for counsel, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, my name is Grant Niemann and I appear with my colleague Mr. Williamson for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: For the Defence please may I have appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, my name is Toma Fila, I am an attorney, I am here with my colleague Miss Jelena Lopicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann and Mr. Fila, this morning we will be hearing a motion filed by the Defence challenging the legality of the arrest of Mr. Dokmanovic. Are you ready to proceed, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, but before that, I would like to say that I withdraw the second motion with regard to the indictment, as regards the imprecision of the indictment. Please consider it invalid because I have written an informal letter to the Prosecution and we have discussed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. That motion challenging the form of the indictment was a part of this motion that you filed challenging the legality of the arrest. That will be considered withdrawn. Thank you. Do you wish to make any opening statement before we proceed with evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like to present my opening statement after the presentation of the evidence, if it pleases the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is acceptable. Mr. Niemann, do you have anything to say at this point or do you wish to await the receipt of evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, there is one matter, if I may raise it at this stage. One of the witnesses that we intend to call today is an interpreter and he operates in the field in Bosnia and in Croatia and Serbia. Because of that we are asking for very limited protective measures, namely that his name not be used in the course of the proceedings. No other protection is sought in relation to him. We have discussed this matter with Mr. Fila and Mr. Fila consents to our application. Your Honours, because of the difficult situation in operating on three sides, we submit that this is an appropriate matter where limited protection, just in the use of the name, would in our submission be appropriate. I have written his name on a piece of paper. If your Honours are disposed to grant the witness this limited protection, then I will hand the note to Mr. Fila and it can then be handed up to your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: He or she will be known as witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Witness A, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: When we hear from that witness, then what we will do is to show the witness a piece of paper and ask him to confirm that that is his name, and otherwise your request will be granted and that witness will be referred to as Witness A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Please, the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, is there any objection to the accused being given the name of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Excuse me a moment. (Pause).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might ask Mr. Williamson to address you on that matter, because that is something that he is peculiarly aware of in view of this particular interpreter's involvement on the day of the arrest. Perhaps I might ask him to address you on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the time of the request the interpreter had requested that the accused not know his name and, in fact, a false name was used in all of his conversations with Mr. Dokmanovic, so it would be our request that he not be provided with the name of the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. I really do not see the need for the accused to know the name of the witness. The purpose of this protective measure, the writing of the name on a piece of paper and the witness confirming that that is his name is for the court, for the Tribunal to make sure that that witness is who he purports to be, so really it is a protection as it relates to -- in terms of identification of the name, it is protection for the court to assure that this person is who he purports to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Dokmanovic would only like to know whether the witness is a male or a female.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: From what I hear he is a male.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: He is a male.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the interpreter depicted on the videotape that Mr. Dokmanovic, the court and Defence counsel have seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That was what I was going to ask you. The request of Prosecution will be granted, the witness will be referred to as Witness A. The court will confirm that that witness is who he purports to be when he is called. Mr. Fila, would you call your first witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The Defence calls Mr. Knezevic. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, would you stand, please? You will be given an oath that I ask you take. MR. MILAN KNEZEVIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, you may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, since we do not have much -- I cannot ask too much questions because we only have one day and I would like to say some time, I would like you to allow me to question this witness only about the circumstances of how he found himself with Mr. Dokmanovic in the critical moment and what happened at that time, so this is only one brief story that I would like to question him about, if that is agreeable to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is, but Mr. Fila, we have as much time as you need. I do not want you to limit your time. We can proceed as late into the evening as is necessary. Fine, you may proceed. Yes, Mr. Fila. Examined by MR. FILA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us a few words about yourself Mr. Knezevic, who you are, how you found yourself with Mr. Dokmanovic, how do you know him, and what happened when you entered into UNTAES?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Milan Knezevic, I was born in 1945 in Dalj. My occupation, I am a teacher, I am a father of two children. I have two sons, one is age 23 and the other one is aged 17. I lived and I worked as a teacher in Darda Republic of Croatia and since 28th May, I have been forced to leave the territory of Croatia because of threats and a list of the Serbs under suspicion. I left my entire property in Croatia. I live in Sombor now and I knew Mr. Dokmanovic from before because we were involved in sports in Slavonija and in Baranja where we both lived and worked. I knew him as an honourable man and a good friend. Since fate has forced us to live in the same town, it was quite normal that we had the occasion to see each other. On that day, that was 26th June 1997, I worked in a rented house in which I lived with my family in Sombor. I was working in the yard, I was mowing the lawn. Mr. Dokmanovic called me on the phone and asked me to come to his place urgently. I thought he wanted me to help him in some way and at 6.10 pm I reached Mr. Dokmanovic's place. He was with a friend, they were having coffee, it was an informal friendly atmosphere and so we talked about freedom of thought and we also discussed politics and sport. Then maybe after 30 minutes of conversation, Mr. Dokmanovic and I quote, he told me, I quote, "my friend, I have a proposal for you, a good idea". Then I learnt that Mr. Dokmanovic offered me a very interesting proposal. He wanted me to go with him to Vukovar the next day and after his explanation I told him very briefly, "Slavko, I still do not trust the Croatian authorities. Even today I do not trust some of the persons from UNTAES, because I have some experience and I am afraid that if we go there, we would be framed". But Mr. Dokmanovic, very persuasively, was trying to make me go and I trust my friend, I trust him even today. He told me that he had guarantees from the secretary, Mr. Michael Hryshchyshyn from the Cabinet of Mr. Klein and then I began to see that there was some justification in what we were talking about. Then he mentioned a man by the name of Kevin Curtis. I had never met that person, I had never heard about that. That was the first time I heard about him. He told me that he had discussions with that man the previous day at his home in Sombor and that he had received guarantees of assurances of safe conduct and that there would be no problems because they would go to Vukovar and back under the protection and control of UNTAES, and I do trust UNTAES in such circumstances. He also told me in the end that Mr. Klein, the chief administrator, he was at the time in New York and he was travelling to Zagreb, that he had assurances from him too. Mr. Klein was travelling to Zagreb and he was supposed to meet Mr. Tudjman and discuss the protection of property of non-amnestied Serbs. Then I saw a document and I believed in that document, and I thought that if we managed to protect the property, our property and the property of the other side, why should we not go and have this discussion? We believed, we thought that Mr. Klein was a very honourable man. I went with Mr. Klein to Zagreb twice in my capacity as the member of the executive counsel, municipal executive council, so I said to Mr. Dokmanovic, "we will see tomorrow. You do not know what is going to happen until tomorrow". So I left Mr. Dokmanovic saying that maybe I will go and maybe I will not, and the next morning we heard each other on the phone and then I said that I would go, because then I believed that what Mr. Kevin Curtis offered was the truth, bearing in mind his function and his position. Mr. Dokmanovic came to my home around 2.15 pm, and it took us about 30 to 40 minutes to reach the bridge on our side, on the Serbian side, by car, and we discussed the lack of security in the place where we were going, because the previous day the court, a court in Croatia convicted an innocent man to five years imprisonment. I knew that person personally, he was innocent, but Mr. Dokmanovic really had an enormous confidence and trust in what the secretary of Mr. Klein and Mr. Kevin Curtis had assured him of and that was the intention of Mr. Klein, to protect us. When we reached the bridge, it was 14.53 hours and the car in which we came was taken over by a friend of Mr. Dokmanovic and a friend of mine, and he took the car to his house for safe keeping, so we crossed the bridge, it was about 14.55 hours. We walked across the bridge. We greeted our customs officials and police officers, they did not check us and then at the distance of about 30 metres, both myself and Mr. Dokmanovic saw two parked cars with UN signs, and as we approached them -- well the distance was about maybe 30 metres -- a man was standing in front of those cars, he was dressed in very elegant manner, he was dark, I would be able to recognise him. He held the badge in his hand and when we reached him, he asked, "Mr. Dokmanovic?", Mr. Dokmanovic nodded, yes, and then he said "You?", and he was told I was a friend and he said okay. On the basis of some of my psychological analysis, I realised that this man did not like the fact that I was there. Mr. Dokmanovic was given a badge which he placed on his left lapel, it was a badge with a colour photograph and I entered the car. Maybe a minute or two later, we started across the bridge at quite high speed. I was sure we were going to Vukovar to talk to Mr. Klein. We were under armed escort, and to the left of me, I sat behind the driver, the window was open and there was a strong draught which bothered me. I tried to close the window with the button. It did not work and at that time I became suspicious, I thought something was going on. I started to suspect that this looked like some kind of -- that I was being detained in some way, and as we approached the border the car slowed down. Towards us, there were some civilians vehicles coming towards us from the direction of Dalj, and the traffic was stopped on that side for a short period and we were able to cross easily. At that time I noticed something that I had never noted before and I had crossed that crossing maybe 200 or 300 times, that everybody saluted the car that we were in, and that gave me some indication that this was a specific situation, probably out of respect for the vehicle owned by Mr. Klein. So we approached the UNTAES checkpoint, which is about a kilometre and a half away from that crossing. The vehicle slowed down and in the opposite direction, in front of the camp, there was a white truck. It was parked there, it was with the UN insignia. I am very familiar with that area because I was born there, as I said, in Dalj. As we approached the camp, going towards the middle area in the camp, the vehicle that was parked to the right went over to the left side, and for a moment it seemed to me that there would be a crash, but our driver swerved into the camp with the frightening screech of the tyres and so now I am coming to a very peculiar element, when the vehicle stopped suddenly there was some masked people armed and we were dragged out of the vehicle and at that moment, we were taken -- one of us were taken to the right side and Mr. Dokmanovic was taken to the left side. At that moment, I felt very unsafe. I was sure that I had been sincere, but that I had allowed myself to be arrested in the territory of my State and to be taken to the other side. My hands were tied behind my back, as were Mr. Dokmanovic's, and I was taken under armed escort to a rather dark container, where I remained from maybe 15.05 hours to maybe 21.00 hours when I was visited by an interpreter from Mr. Klein's office, and a person who I assume is from Mr. Klein's office that deals with legal affairs. I was told then that I was arrested by mistake and that I would be released and taken to our side of the border. That is how it happened. I was taken across to halfway across the bridge and I went back to our side on foot. As for Mr. Dokmanovic, I did not know where he was, nor was I told. The only thing I was told was that there would be an indictment against Mr. Dokmanovic on the basis of a well kept secret under seal, as a movement in chess, to be activated the moment he moves to the Serb territory. Your Honour, I would like to end my presentation with this opinion stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, do you have an additional question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination? Cross-examined by MR. WILLIAMSON

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, my name is Clint Williamson, I am an attorney from the Prosecutor's office. How long have you known Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have known Mr. Dokmanovic from the 80s, in mid 80s, maybe 1984, 1985.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were involved in some sport activities with him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of sports was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Soccer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you consider him to be a good friend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I considered him to be a good friend after several years of our co-operation in the field of sports. I got to know his style and his character and yes, I do claim that he was a good friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On 27th June when you travelled with him to the bridge at Bogojevo, were you aware that he had a weapon with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to the border post you indicated that you spoke to the Serbian customs officers and then walked about 30 metres past the border post in the direction of Croatia and got in the vehicles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct that I greeted the customs officials and the police forces. It is good manners and proper behaviour, and also with the question, "do you want our ID on the way there or back", it was not a conversation, just a question as we were walking past. One of the duty officers waved us through. I did not stay there to talk to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you spoke to them, just passed your greetings, you said you walked about 30 metres past the border post to get into the vehicle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the place --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: He never said across the border, this is not correct. Objection, the witness never said that he had crossed the border. He simply never said it. You have to know the bridge, the UNTAES vehicles are on the territory of Yugoslavia, not across the border. The witness never said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I did not ask that either. I asked him if he passed the border post and walked 30 metres to get into the vehicles; is that correct, Mr. Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not able to understand the question. If you do not mind repeating the question once again?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Where were the vehicles located in relation to the border post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In relation to the border post where the vehicles were, there were about 30 metres, 30 or 40 metres around that from the place where our police forces were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which direction, 30 metres or 40 metres in which direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the direction between Bogojevo and Erdut, that is the direction from the Serb side, from our Serb side, the Yugoslav side, towards the Republic of Croatia and to the border crossing, there is still about a kilometre and a half to two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that from the border post, Bogojevo is in one direction, Erdut is in the other direction, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the vehicles located on the side toward Erdut or on the side toward Bogojevo in relation to the border post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In relation to the ramp where the police are on the guard, the vehicle was facing Erdut, was turned towards the direction of Erdut, to be concrete on the left bank of the Danube where we were, there was a vehicle still inside of the territory and on the right bank, across the Danube. That is the territory of Croatia and the territory of Erdut. The vehicle was on our side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand it was on that side of the river, but I am asking you, had the vehicles passed the border post or were they still on the other side of the border post, on the side in the direction of Erdut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to duty regulations, vehicles cannot go across when they want to the territory of one or the other State. That is done with a special permit with an explanation as to why that is done and if the vehicle had requested it in that case, it would have no longer been able to drive across the way Dokmanovic and Knezevic were driven across.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did not answer my question: was the vehicle located on the side of the border post in the direction of Erdut, on the Erdut side of the border post? It is a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the side of Erdut. I said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to what Mr. Dokmanovic told you about his assurances from Mr. Hryshcyhshyn and from General Klein, this information you have received only from Mr. Dokmanovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had not spoken of that with anybody else, nor would I want to speak about that with anybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not present when the telephone call was placed between Mr. Dokmanovic and Mr. Hryshcyhshyn; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not present for any of the conversations between Mr. Dokmanovic and Mr. Curtis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, do you have additional questions? Re-examined by MR. FILA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one to clarify as to why did Mr. Knezevic need assurances to cross the border. Is he on any list of the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I answer? I am on the list of unwanted non-amnestied Serbs of number 147 decision of the Republic of Croatia and I am under investigation on the basis of Article 122 of the penal code of the Republic of Croatia, which is a crime against war prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you have crossed the border unless you had these guarantees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us clarify this: where is the border between Croatia and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The border between Yugoslavia and Croatia is along the river Danube.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On which side were the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The vehicles were on the left side of the Danube, on the side of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, I have just a couple of questions. You testified that Mr. Dokmanovic showed you a document when you visited him on June 26th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I testified that Mr. Dokmanovic showed me a document, no document was shown to me on 26th June, so that is the day when I went to Mr. Dokmanovic, only to talk to him to obtain information and for him to persuade me to take the journey with him the following day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it that Mr. Dokmanovic showed you a document? I understood that you visited him on June 26th, came to his house about 6.10, talked with him and then he showed you some document. Maybe I misunderstood your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No document was shown to me by Mr. Dokmanovic. Perhaps what you remember is the following, the moment Mr. Dokmanovic telephoned me and invited me, he told me to come over to his home to speak with me and to show me something, but there was something said but nothing shown.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then it was at 2.15, I gather, on June 26th that Mr. Dokmanovic came to your house and then you were driven to the bridge on the side of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct, Mr. Dokmanovic was very precise at 2.15 with the sound of the siren he announced his arrival, I was prepared, I was waiting for him. I picked up my bag and I went outside, locked my house and went to the vehicle at 2.15 pm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This vehicle was, I gather, driven by a friend of yours or Mr. Dokmanovic, they then drove you, he or she drove you to the bridge; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct that Mr. Dokmanovic and I were alone on our way to Bogojevo and in a camping area. We stopped at a place where his friend Mr. Bozidar Purkovic lived. We stopped by to pick him up. Mr. Dokmanovic continued to drive to the bridge, turned the vehicle, and when he left the vehicle, he gave the steering wheel to Mr. Purkovic, who officially then returned the vehicle back and parked it by his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You and Mr. Dokmanovic walked across the bridge. Did you then walk through the customs point that was manned by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Customs point and the police station or command post are connected, they are one next to the other. So when I crossed the customs and the police point, yes, they were about 10 or 15 metres behind us when you drive across with the vehicle because an UNTAES vehicle is not allowed to cross to the other side without special permission from UNTAES.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The customs point, is that the point after which you pass through, you are on Croatian -- the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is our Yugoslav side. As I said, we had about a kilometre and a half to the Croatian territory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a Croatian customs point on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Looking towards Erdut it is about a kilometre and a half, yes, on the other side of the river, at the right bank of Danube. It was inland about 500 metres, the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you were picked up in the UNTAES vehicles, was it -- which side was it with respect to the Croatian customs point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were on the left bank, which means on the side of Yugoslavia and Serbia, on the Bogojevo side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So I gather there is a point, there is an area on the bridge over the Danube between the Croatian customs point and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia customs point, so that you go through the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's customs point, then you go for a period of time over the bridge and then at another point you cross through the Croatian customs point; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try to be original from the place of the arrest, my arrest, because that was when we were locked into the vehicle, it was clear to me later but not at that moment, if I had wanted to leave the vehicle, I was unable to. I was simply forced to go across. I am speaking on my personal behalf. To the border line there is about 700 or 800 metres, that is to the middle of the Danube River and the bridge. I do not know if I am being clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is a Croatian customs point on one side, I gather, of the bridge and then there is a Federal Republic of Yugoslavia customs point. Then in between the two customs points is a length of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know at what point you are in Croatian territory or territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, having passed through the customs point of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and not having passed through the Croatian customs point, how do you know whether you are in Croatian territory or territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia while you are on this bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very simple, I officially feel crossing into the Republic of Croatia when I am as a citizen and a passenger crossing the middle of the bridge and approaching the right bank of Danube. Once I am in the right bank of Danube, I am already 500 or 600 metres into the territory of Croatia, because the border line is along the middle of the Danube River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you have to determine where the middle of the river is, and once you are on one side of the middle of the river, you are either in Croatian territory or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, depending on what side you are with respect to the middle of the river?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what the regulations say. That is not what I say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Fila, do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps, if it pleases the court, I want to explain something. The bridge does not go just across the river --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It is inappropriate for you to testify, that is why we have a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No. All right then I will ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is why I asked the witness. He has explained it well. If you wish to ask him additional questions, ask him the questions and then we will hear from him. Further re-examined by MR. FILA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it please the court, I would just like to ask one question: were the UNTAES vehicles on the part of the bridge that is over the river or on the part of the bridge that was over land?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both vehicles were on the territory of the Republic of Yugoslavia on the shore on the bank, on the part where the bridge is over the land and not over the water.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That is what I wanted to explain. And another question, how were they dressed? If it pleases the court, that is what I have forgotten. What were they wearing, you and Mr. Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember very well that I was wearing a summer shirt with short sleeves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And Dokmanovic was wearing a suit, a suit similar to the one I am wearing with a tie.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have nothing else, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mr. Knezevic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, you are permanently excused. That means you are free to leave. You understand the limitations that govern your presence here so I understand you will then be leaving and returning to where you came from. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, would you call your next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I would like to call the wife of Mr. Dokmanovic, Mrs. Danilka Dokmanovic. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mrs. Dokmanovic, would you please stand? You will be handed an oath for you to take. MRS. DANILKA DOKMANOVIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, you may be seated. Mr. Fila? Miss Lopicic? Examined by MS. LOPICIC

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The counsel has not turned the microphone on.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOPICIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Dokmanovic, could you please tell us something about yourself, who you are, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Danilka Dokmanovic, born on 24th October 1949 in Vukovar. I am the wife of Slavko Dokmanovic. I hold a degree in commerce. I am a mother of two. At the moment I reside in Sombor in Vojvodjanska Street, number 35. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, thank you. I also wanted to ask you if you know Mr. Curtis and his interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have Mr. Curtis and his interpreter visited your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that happened and what you talked about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let us make sure that we do not mention the name of that interpreter. Mrs. Dokmanovic, before you came into court an agreement was reached between counsel that the name of that interpreter will not be mentioned so do not mention his name, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOPICIC
utterances.text: All right, just the interpreter, without mentioning his name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the first name they visited the house where I live on 24th June 1997. I was at work, but Slavko told me that people from the Tribunal were to come at 10.00 to the house where we lived. I returned home about 2.10 in the afternoon and I met two men there, talking to my husband. On that day they stayed about 4.20, 4.30 in the afternoon, I am not exactly sure about the time. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what they talked about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They talked about the events in Vukovar, mainly before the war broke out, while my husband was still in Vukovar, while he was still allowed access.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you learn that your husband was to travel on Friday 27th to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 26th when I returned from work the people from the Tribunal had already left and Slavko told me that on 27th June he was going to go to Vukovar to meet Mr. Klein. I tried to persuade him not to go, I told him not to go. I told him it was not safe, but he told me that he had arranged everything, that Mr. Curtis had put him in contact with Mr. Klein's secretary, Mr. Michael Hryshcyhshyn, who guaranteed security, who guaranteed safe journey there and return to Sombor. I tried to persuade him not to go once again, but when he explained to me that everything is arranged, that they told him they would send the General's vehicles to pick him up, vehicles which are safe and known to the checkpoints and not stopped, that would be quite safe. I also believed that, believing that Mr. Klein is there, in that territory, to protect us and so Slavko left for Vukovar on the 27th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will give you a note that I have given to the court. If you can explain to us the meaning of this note?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Can we mark that as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOPICIC
utterances.text: This document is already on the files as evidence and it has been translated to the English language. The Defence has provided a translation. Here is a copy in English, the paper is -- the slip of paper is an original and this is a photocopy. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Miss Lopicic, the document that has been handed to the witness will be marked as Defence Exhibit 1 and then the English translation will be 1A. I understand that they are a part of documents that have been submitted to the Registry this morning, but I think it is appropriate to make them a part of the record for this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOPICIC
utterances.text: The documents have been submitted and the Defence submitted this on Friday, but we added the translation to it and we submitted this to the Registry this morning. Could you explain to me exactly what is on this piece of paper and who wrote this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was written by Slavko before he went to meet Mr. Klein because I did not see him at home that day because since I had been at work and the gentleman from the Tribunal was supposed to meet him at our house at 7.00 in the evening the same day, and since Slavko thought that he could be late, he wrote: "Danilka, if I am not there by 7.00 in the evening and if I do not call you, please call me on the above phone number", which is the number of Mr. Klein's secretary and that is the number that is in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you concluded that that was when he was supposed to meet Klein?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOPICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Defence Exhibit 1A?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: They will be admitted. Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: After learning that Mr. Dokmanovic had been arrested, did the witness go to see Mr. Klein and if so, what did they talk about on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, only one counsel may question the witness. If there is another question that you wish to put to the witness, then let Miss Lopicic do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOPICIC
utterances.text: So I will ask Mrs. Dokmanovic one more question. After your husband was arrested, did you go to meet Mr. Klein, General Klein, and if so, when and explain the contents of your conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I asked him to see me. He saw me on 2nd July and the conversation was mainly with me asking how he could have provided guarantees of safety to my husband who was eventually arrested and who could have done that on his behalf for his authority to be ridiculed in this way, and then he explained to me that he had to co-operate with the Tribunal, that that was the agreement, and this is what he said to me, "if I had not arrested him, I could have started packing my bags within 48 hours". That was his answer to my questions and I had no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOPICIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Dokmanovic. That will be all for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Any cross-examination? Cross-examined by MR. WILLIAMSON

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions, your Honour. Mrs. Dokmanovic, my name is Clint Williamson, I am one of the attorneys from the Prosecutor's Office. You were not present when your husband had any of the discussions with Mr. Curtis about the arrangements for him to go to Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not present when your husband spoke with Mr. Hryshcyhshyn on the telephone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not present, but my sister-in-law was there. She served him coffee at the time when Mr. -- when Slavko talked to Mr. Hryshcyhshyn over the phone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But all of the information you have received in regard to what assurances he may or may not have received have been given to you by him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By him and by my sister-in-law, because she was present, she was there when the gentleman from the Tribunal said, having talked -- when Slavko talked to Mr. Hryshcyhshyn, this gentleman from the Tribunal said "there is nothing for you to fear because everything will be all right".

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Miss Lopicic?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOPICIC
utterances.text: No further questions for Mrs. Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mrs. Dokmanovic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mrs. Dokmanovic, you are permanently excused, that means you are free to leave. Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, do you have additional witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Our last witness to conclude things within the two hours as I promised, that is Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic, who will testify as to who told him what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. We will stand in recess for 20 minutes and then we will hear from Mr. Dokmanovic. (11.05 am) (A short break) (11.25 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, would you call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The Defence calls its next witness, Mr. Dokmanovic, Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic? MR. SLAVKO DOKMANOVIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dokmanovic, you may be seated. Mr. Fila, I understand Mr. Dokmanovic now will be testifying only about the circumstances surrounding the arrest. That will be the limited purpose of this testimony. Examined by MR. FILA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, that is how I understood. Mr. Dokmanovic, please, can you tell us something about yourself to begin with, but if you could wait with your answer for a while so that my question can be translated into English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Slavko Dokmanovic, I was born on 14th December 1949 in Trpinja. I graduated from the Faculty of Agriculture in Osijek and I worked in agriculture, agri business in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will ask you just a few questions regarding the circumstances of your arrest. Until what time were you involved in the assembly of Vukovar as the President of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was the President of the Municipal Assembly in Vukovar until 5th April 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that close to the UNTAES base in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that time did you contact the UNTAES officials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Virtually every day, because they were located in the Vukovar municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after your --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left in July, but I returned because my house was in Trpinja. I do not recall the exact date when I was there for the last time, but I was employed until 5th October 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you have somebody, some of your relations who lived in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have a house there and my son and his wife lived there and my grandson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is: how did you come into contact with the officials from the Tribunal? When was the first time and in what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the proposal of my friend, Mr. Milinkovic and another friend of mine, Mr. Savic, I got in touch with the officials of the Tribunal, their office in Belgrade and the first meeting took place in the beginning of 1997, somewhere in the vicinity of Belgrade. I do not recall the exact name of the village. I met a woman whose name I cannot recall now in the house of Mr. Milinkovic and after that I was in touch with the representatives of the Tribunal in the office in Vukovar. That was a few telephone calls. It all happened in the spring of this year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you come to meet Mr. Curtis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a few telephone calls with Mr. Curtis before we actually met. We first met on 24th June this year in my house in Sombor in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your status in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a refugee in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose passport do you have and where have your ID been issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am treated as a refugee. I have an ID card issued in Yugoslavia, I do not have a passport. I have an old passport issued some time in the 80s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where has it been issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose citizenship do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have a citizenship, I am a refugee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose citizenship did you have before that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yugoslav, and as to the republic we did not have citizenship of the Republic, so I had citizenship of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to your contact with Mr. Curtis. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 24th June, after the telephone call, Mr. Curtis came to my place as we agreed, we agreed that he would arrive at 10 am. I think he arrived a few minutes earlier with an interpreter, I let them in, and we talked from 10.00 until about 4.00 pm, about things that happened in Vukovar in 1990 and 1991, and towards the end of our discussion I asked Mr. Curtis whether, as part of the authority -- whether the Tribunal is also authorised to solve issues regarding the property of Serbs not covered with the amnesty and of those Serbs who are unable and unwilling to live in the territory under the control of UNTAES, and what would happen with that property, because for most of the people this was the only property they had, and Mr. Curtis told me it was not within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal, but he said that it was under the jurisdiction of UNTAES and he offered to me, after I told him that I was no longer in touch with UNTAES, he offered that he would organise a meeting with the representatives of UNTAES, that is with General Klein, with regard to solving the issue of this property. Since we agreed about that he told me that he would let me know the next day when the meeting was scheduled for, and that was 25th June 1997. After that, Mr. Curtis left, together with his interpreter. That was some time after 4.00 pm. The next day we had arranged to meet again the next day, that was on the 25th, the same time, the same place and Mr. Curtis arrived with his interpreter, and then when we entered the house he told me that he had some good news, that he had talked to Mr. Michael Hryshcyhshyn, that Mr. Hryshcyhshyn was expecting my phone call at about 10.15 and that was approximately the time when we were having this discussion. He gave me a slip of paper with the name. I think it is part of the record --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just a moment. With your permission, your Honours, I would like to present this slip of paper, a copy has been submitted this morning, together with the other documents, for identification purposes. Then I would like to have it -- to offer it into evidence. (Handed). Did he say what was the slip of paper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me to call the phone numbers that are listed here and then I phoned these numbers and a woman answered. I told her who I was and she put me through to Mr. Hryshcyhshyn. I talked with Mr. Hryshcyhshyn for about ten minutes. I told him what this was all about. Mr. Hryshcyhshyn told me that he had spoken to Mr. Curtis and that Mr. Curtis had relayed to him that I would like to see Mr. Klein. I said that that was correct, and then he told me that he had talked to Mr. Klein and that he has been authorised by Mr. Klein to arrange a meeting with me. I said that it was all right, but that the meeting should take place in the territory of Yugoslavia, since I did not feel safe in the territory of Croatia. Mr. Hryshcyhshyn told me that Mr. Klein proposed that the meeting took place in Vukovar, since he had to apply for a special permission to cross into Yugoslavia, so I said "all right, if that is the case, but then I demand to be given assurances of safe conduct, both there and back again into Yugoslavia", and Mr. Hryshcyhshyn told me this is understood: "We guarantee full safety to you both on the way there and back; we will send a vehicle for you, a special vehicle that is used by Mr. Klein. Everybody recognises that vehicle and that vehicle is not stopped anywhere". I said that that vehicle has to pick me up in the territory of Yugoslavia -- I apologise, I am sorry, Mr. Hryshcyhshyn also told me that he had a message for me from Mr. Klein, that Mr. Klein would be very glad to see me and that Mr. Klein has certain photographs from the previous meetings to give to me. Mr. Klein came to the territory controlled by UNTAES at the moment, because we asked for it and I had full trust in Mr. Klein, because he is the emperor, he is the chief there and if I cannot trust Mr. Klein having participated in all the meetings, how can the 150,000 people who live there trust him? So I did not suspect anything, and after I concluded the conversation Mr. Curtis asked me if everything was all right, and I said, "we will see" and Mr. Curtis said, "do not worry, you will have all the assurances and guarantees. Everything will be all right". Then we concluded the conversation, because I had some guests who arrived at the time. Mr. Curtis said that he would like to leave and I took that to be a sign of his good manners and he explained that he was leaving because of the guests so to allow me ample time to be with my guests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment. When you asked for the guarantees, did you seek guarantees for one specific State? Did you ask guarantees not to be arrested by martians, Chinese, Japanese?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I asked for guarantees of safe conduct to and back to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, he left at about 2.00 pm and we agreed to meet again on Friday 27th June at 7.00 at the place, at the house where I live, after my return from Vukovar. Mr. Curtis knew at that time that I would not be coming back from Vukovar, but that is another story. Mr. Curtis left and at about 3.30 I had a phone call from a person who said he was from UNTAES and he asked me whether I needed a vehicle to come and fetch me in Sombor. I said no, that I would be coming to the bridge with my friends and that it was sufficient for them to send the vehicle to the bridge. Then the next day on Thursday, that was the 26th at about 7.00 pm, I called Mr. Knezevic, who is from Baranja. He has had some experience, and he is a very well known and respected person in this area and he is in a similar situation as I am. I asked him to come to my place to arrange something. After about 10 minutes, because we live close by, Mr. Knezevic arrived. I was in the back yard with a friend of mine, Mr. Purkovic. Mr. Knezevic sat next to us, we talked for a while and then I explained what this was about. I told him this concerned the property of about 15,000 Serbs or maybe even more, and that it also concerned our property, and that both of us knew Mr. Klein and that I suggested that I had actually arranged to meet Mr. Klein on Friday the 27th June, and I asked him to accompany me, because he also knew Mr. Klein since he held an office while the executive council of the area was in existence. He also knows Baranja. Baranja is on one side and Srem is on the other side. He was able to see the situation, to analyse the situation. He was reluctant because there was a list of about 150 people who are not covered by amnesty from Croatia, and he asked me, I quote, "Slavko, is it safe?" I said, "it is safe, Mr. Klein guarantees our safety. If the two of us cannot trust Mr. Klein, then who will trust him in this area?" Then reluctantly, he probably had some premonition, but he is a brave man, he agreed. Mr. Knezevic left soon after that, because he said he had some unfinished business at home. We arranged that I would pick him up tomorrow on Friday 27th at 2.15 pm, because it was arranged that a UNTAES vehicle would be waiting for us at the Yugoslav side at around 3.0 pm. At 2.15, I came to pick up Mr. Knezevic. I honked the horn. He was ready, he left the house, he entered the vehicle and we set off towards the bridge, towards the border. There is a camping area immediately in front of the bridge and I had agreed with Mr. Purkovic, who had attended our discussion when we arranged that meeting, I asked him to accompany us to the border so as to return the vehicle. I told him that we would pick him up and that we would all go back on our way back. Mr. Purkovic got into the vehicle and we started -- the distance is about 500 or 600 metres, this camping area is about 600 metres away from the border. We reached the border crossing, and then I noticed two vehicles on my left, stationary vehicles and I commented, I said "these guys are really precise". I turned the vehicle at the exit towards the bridge, that is about 20 metres away and I parked it there near the bridge. Mr. Knezevic and myself got out of the car. Mr. Purkovic sat at the steering wheel and drove the vehicle back to his home. Mr. Knezevic and myself, we started walking towards the parked vehicles. We greeted the men, I mean the police and the customs officers, and we started walking towards the vehicles. The vehicles were facing the Croatian side. In the first vehicle that we passed by, and these were two white Jeeps with large and clearly visible UN insignia, in the first vehicle that escorted us there were some soldiers, the windows were tinted, but we could see the silhouettes, and in between those two vehicles there was a man who was walking towards us and he asked us whether we spoke English. We said who we were, he asked whether we spoke English and we said no and he put a badge on me, and as for Mr. Knezevic, he had not been announced, so he did not get a badge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please describe the badge? What was written on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember what was written on the badge, but it indicated that it was me. I cannot remember what was written, I did not even look. But it was probably something that I could use to identify myself if the need arose. This gentleman who met us there, he indicated that we should enter the vehicle and we did so. This vehicle also had tinted windows. We started moving at a pretty high speed and Mr. Knezevic commented that the Danube was quite high. We crossed the bridge quite soon and the vehicle slowed down on the Croatian side, on the checkpoint there, but we did not stop. Then there is the road climbs up, but the vehicle continued at a high speed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Dokmanovic, did something happen with the vehicle when you entered the vehicle, something with the door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The door locked. We could hear the click.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To our left as you climb this slope, there is a gas station that has been turned into a fortification, I do not know what the purpose is of this building. It is a UNTAES facility that is surrounded with sandbags. From the other side, from the opposite direction, a truck also bearing UN insignia started driving towards us and since we were driving at high speed we almost crashed. Our driver swerved sharply to the left towards the gas station, and the vehicle tipped, I even thought that we would tip over, and then the vehicle stopped suddenly. A large number of soldiers ran towards us, they wore masks on their faces and they had automatic rifles pointed at us, automatic weapons I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, what did you say at that time? We now heard the description, please do not continue, because this is confidential, but can you tell us what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well that is what we saw. We did not see my first reaction, because when they opened the door and started to drag me and Mr. Knezevic out, I said, "this is a mistake, we are going to meet Mr. Klein".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This has not been recorded. Did you repeat that on several occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must have repeated that two or three times. I asked them to allow me to call Mr. Klein on the phone, but they did not allow me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you carry a gun, Mr. Dokmanovic? Do you have a permit for that gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the bag that was next to me on the floor there was a pistol. This pistol was in the bag for a long time, and the newspaper that is also in the bag can prove at what time I placed this pistol in the bag. I do not carry this bag with me all the time, I just took it with me so that I can put my notebook in it. I have a permit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in other words, the pistol was not -- you did not carry the pistol on your person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you endanger anyone with the pistol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, and I never fired this gun at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please describe the bridge? What does this bridge look like, what part of the bridge is over the river? Is there a part that is not over the river? Where were the vehicles parked, over land or over water, and on whose territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bridge is about 2 kilometres long, because the Danube is about a kilometre wide at that point. It depends, of course, on the level of water. At least about 500 metres on the Yugoslav side is over land, over swamp. It has been sanded over. On the left side there is a camping area and on the right side there are warehouses with silos which are over land, so this is over land, not over water. The border before and now runs along the middle of the Danube River.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the border between the Socialist Republic of Croatia and Serbia in the time of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in this area, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is guarding the border, police or army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there a patrol, is there a sentry post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is a patrol and they patrol daily, and closer to the Danube, I cannot tell you more precisely now how far away from the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this area, there is a sentry post, sentry house. Now, in relation to that sentry post where were the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the Yugoslav side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now say that they were between the area that is patrolled and the police post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the soldiers were -- the army was closer to the Croatian side, so they had crossed the border, so they had crossed this area that is controlled by the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I go back now for a moment? What was the reason why you were no longer the President of the Municipal Assembly after 5th October?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the reasons was that not everybody agreed with the Erdut agreement that had been signed. There were quite a few conflicts with regard to that, but there were probably some other reasons too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back now to the most important thing. Why did you go to Croatia? Let us repeat for the umpteenth time, what were the guarantees that were given to you, that you got guarantees not to be arrested by Croats or by anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked to be given safe conduct both to that area and back to the territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it had nothing to do with who might endanger you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was on the list of the Serbs who had not been granted amnesty by the Croats, but there was this joint police force there. I was not familiar with the situation fully, but I asked for safe conduct there and back to Yugoslavia, both for myself and for Mr. Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. This is all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson, do you have cross-examination? Cross-examined by MR. WILLIAMSON

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Mr. Dokmanovic, the last statement you made is that you had asked for safe conduct to Vukovar and back to Yugoslavia for you and Mr. Knezevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For myself. At the time Mr. Knezevic was not mentioned. When I asked permit, I asked for one for myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you ask for safe conduct for Mr. Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not ask for safe conduct for Mr. Knezevic, as I said. That goes without saying. I believe that since I had one he would automatically have one, since he was with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was just a misstatement at the end of your direct examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On 27th June you believed that you were going directly to a meeting with General Klein and back; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until that time you trusted General Klein?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I trusted him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had no reason to believe that he would be untruthful with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were on the way to this meeting, were you relaxed about it, were you comfortable with going to see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand this question. I was going to a meeting. I cannot really describe my state of mind at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any anxiety about the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it is very straightforward. Were you anxious or upset or anxious about this meeting in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly was not completely relaxed about it. It was definitely something that was new and it was not a simple situation, but I believed that things that I was told would eventually be fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you were crossing over the bridge, you indicated that you and Mr. Knezevic talked about the Danube River being high; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was something that Mr. Knezevic alone said, but maybe I really do not remember whether I said, "yes, it is". It is possible I confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any other discussion between you and Mr. Knezevic during the course of the trip?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think not. I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But up until the point in time when you were actually removed from the vehicle, you still believed you were going to a meeting with General Klein; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were shocked when you were taken out of the vehicle, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described General Klein as the emperor, as the chief of the area, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the chief administrator, i.e. the highest authority in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you respect him in that position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was doing the job and it was the duty of all to respect what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever have any reason to fear him personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, or no: did you fear him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This friend that you entrusted your car to, Mr. Purkovic, he was a good friend of yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was quite a good friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He is somebody that you trusted. You gave him the keys to your car and let him drive your car off, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Fila? Further re-examined by MR. FILA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just as a point of clarification, according to him, how much time passed from the moment when he entered the car on the Serb side, on the bridge, until the moment when he was pulled out of the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Williamson?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Just one question. Mr. Dokmanovic, as I understand it, you wanted to discuss issues involving property that belonged to Serbs in Eastern Slavonija.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were told that in order to discuss those issues you had to go to Eastern Slavonija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but I was told that there would be a meeting with Mr. Klein in Vukovar in Eastern Slavonija, since General Klein would require a special permit to cross into Yugoslavia. I do not know if that is correct or not. I was told that I was guaranteed safe conduct, and that is something I have described.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that you could discuss these property issues in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with Mr. Klein?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand. What was I to understand? I just do not understand the question. Could we talk in another place? But the meeting had been arranged for Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you wanted to go, as I understand it, to meet with Mr. Klein to discuss the resolution of these property issues that related to Serb property, I gather, in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to talk about solutions to how to resolve compensation for property for Serbs who cannot, or do not wish to live in the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you make this request to meet with whoever had authority to discussion these issues, or did someone else make the request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I requested that through Mr. Curtis; or rather Mr. Curtis said that that was the responsibility of UNTAES and not the Tribunal. I described this conversation, and that he would try to organise this meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was acceptable with you, I gather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were people coming from institutions that are respected. I never doubted the words of the people who promised me this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, do you have additional questions? Further re-examined by MR. FILA

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, but again just to clarify, were you supposed about your private property and the property of Mr. Knezevic, because that is what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among other things, our private properties as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That would be all. Your Honour, I have no further witnesses, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let me see if Mr. Williamson has any questions. Further cross-examined by MR. WILLIAMSON

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have a couple of questions. Mr. Dokmanovic, you indicated that you received information that General Klein could not come to Serbia because he needed some type of special permit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what Mr. Hryshcyhshyn said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall exactly what he said in that regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me that Mr. Klein was proposing a meeting in Vukovar since in order to cross into Yugoslavia he required a permit. He did not indicate a permit from whom and I did not ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I do not have anything further, your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In the evidence package that I had submitted, there are also the ID card, copy of the passport and all other relevant documents, including this slip, the note that Mr. Hryshcyhshyn gave, so would you like me to read it or should I just leave it for you to read later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: We may have to admit those. Just one question: Mr. Dokmanovic, did you understand that Mr. Klein had authority to discuss these property issues that you were concerned about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the explanation that Mr. Curtis gave to me. This is the responsibility of UNTAES and I would try to arrange a meeting with UNTAES to discuss this. When I told so to Mr. Hryshcyhshyn in a telephone conversation, he answered with, "a good question". Upon his return from New York, Mr. Klein would stop to visit Mr. Tudjman and then he would have the right information to relay to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you knew then if you wanted to discuss these property issues with Mr. Klein you had to go to Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the territories controlled by UNTAES. That is the territory that belonged to Croatia but it is controlled by UNTAES.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you knew if you wanted to discuss these property issues with Mr. Klein, you had to go then to Eastern Slavonija?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what Mr. Hryshcyhshyn suggested, that we talk in Vukovar or rather that that was the suggestion of Mr. Klein which was relayed to me by Mr. Hryshcyhshyn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay, fine thank you. Do you wish to offer Defence Exhibit 2, that is the piece of paper, Mr. Fila, that Mr. Dokmanovic identified? Any objection, Mr. Williamson?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit 2 will be admitted. Mr. Fila, do you need Mr. Dokmanovic now to offer the additional exhibits that you want to offer for this hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No, thank you. The evidence is contained in the package. I do not need it, the family needs it. No, this was a joke. This evidence is something you need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay, very good. Mr. Dokmanovic, you may return to your seat. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What exhibits do you wish to offer, Mr. Fila? We will mark them beginning I suppose with Defence 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: My colleague Jelena will be speaking since this is in English so it is easier for her.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOPICIC
utterances.text: I gave you all the documents in the bag. I would like to explain. The first document is passport of Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is that one exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOPICIC
utterances.text: Yes. That would be exhibit number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: What is your next one?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOPICIC
utterances.text: The next one is firearm permit of Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic that shows that he had also a permit at the time he was illegally arrested. The third item is identification card, personal card of Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic, that was issued on July 22nd 1996 by Vukovar Municipality. The next item is --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOKMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic, can you hear me? Mr. Fila? Mr. Fila, you will have to put your earphones on, I suppose. If Mr. Dokmanovic wishes to say anything he should motion you, rather than speaking out loud, so Mr. Dokmanovic, if you wish to say anything to counsel, just motion him, I look at you. There is a guard sitting next to you and will give your counsel an opportunity to approach you and discuss anything. Please do not exclaim out loud. Defence 5 was -- you had identified that as the identification card for Mr. Dokmanovic, that was when he said no, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOPICIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, it is made in Sombor but Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the stamp is of Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. One moment, I would like to explain that to Mr. Dokmanovic, I am sorry. It was a mistake, it was not issued in Vukovar, I am sorry. The next item is employment card of Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic. I also have the original one, the original card. On page 8, it is important for the Defence, we can see that he worked in Vukovar until October 5th 1996, so that is four months after the warrant of arrest was issued, and given to UNTAES in Croatia. Next item is certificate from Ministry of Internal Affairs of Serbia, where it says that he has a residency in Vojvodjanska Street 35 from July 22nd 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? From where, residence?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOPICIC
utterances.text: That Slavko Dokmanovic has residence in Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in Vojvodjanska Street in Sombor from July 22nd 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The one issued in Vukovar until 5th October? You said he was employed in Vukovar until 5th October. There is a lag of three months.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOPICIC
utterances.text: Yes, but he travelled every day because he was employed until 1996, we have a document, until 1996, October 5th, but his wife moved to Sombor on July 22nd. Shall I go on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Yes. That is 7, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOPICIC
utterances.text: The question is question relating to the case of Adolf Eichman, that is in English language, issued by security council. This is the a digs. It is one page, on the left is English, on the right is French version.
