utterances.text: Your Honour, I would agree that 20.2 arguably would allow the Prosecutor to make arrests, or at least to take persons into custody, which is, in effect, what occurred here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It is your position then that it was a joint arrest, that both UNTAES and the OTP, Office of the Prosecutor, arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: My position is that UNTAES military personnel physically placed Mr. Dokmanovic under arrest. They physically removed him from the vehicle, searched him, placed handcuffs on him. At that point in time, an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor advised Mr. Dokmanovic of his rights and he was transported, together with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and UNTAES military personnel to an airport in Croatia from which he departed to fly to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Then when he departed from Croatia he was in an aeroplane with just Prosecution personnel and two pilots, who I gather were UNTAES people, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Belgian airforce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay, whatever. At least at that point they were solely -- Mr. Dokmanovic was solely in the custody of the Prosecution's office until he arrived in Holland and then he was turned over to the Dutch police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: So there was a joint arrest, is that what you are saying? Are you saying that UNTAES detained him, obtained physical control over him and then the arrest took place when the reading of the rights occurred and that that was accomplished by the Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would say that is when the arrest was completed, at the present he was advised of his rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: And the Prosecution did that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If UNTAES had never appeared on the scene, would the Prosecutor have the authority to detain and arrest Mr. Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would say that they would, again under Rule 59 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Supported by?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Article 20.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Something in the statute. Excuse me then. I interrupted you because you were talking about that point and it seemed to me that differed from the testimony of the witness from the transitional administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would also argue that Mr. Hryshchyshyn is not in a position to speak for UNTAES as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Then do not invite him here to speak. You have other people who can tell us, with the greatest deal of authority, about UNTAES, but this is the only person we have. That is why I asked him those questions. I think it is unfair to offer a witness from UNTAES and then say, "He is not really competent to tell us what we want to know". We need to have people here who are competent, but go ahead, Mr. Williamson.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The next issue, I think, that was raised by Mr. Fila had to do with the sovereignty of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. You have heard testimony that a complaint was forwarded to UNTAES by Mr. Milutinovic, the Foreign Minister. According to Mr. Hryshchyshyn's testimony, there were further discussions at which Mr. Milutinovic was present and President Milosevic was present. This issue was raised and apparently it was resolved in the discussions that took place. It is the submission of the Prosecutor that Mr. Dokmanovic has no standing to raise this issue. If there is an issue of sovereignty, this is an issue between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Tribunal. It has nothing to do with Mr. Dokmanovic. He cannot assert rights as an individual for a State. I think all of the case law maintains this. Mr. Fila has provided to the court a Security Council resolution which was adopted in relation to the arrest of Adolf Eichman by Israeli agents when he was abducted, removed from Argentina and flown back to Israel. The Security Council criticised Israel for this action, but more tellingly, the court in Israel upheld this action. Mr. Eichman subsequently was put on trial and was executed. All of the case law consistently has upheld this. Again and again the position of the courts has been that individuals cannot assert the right of sovereignty. In relation to his comment that Croatia had protested the arrest, Mr. Dokmanovic was transited through Croatian territory. He left from an airport outside of Osijek where Croatian police were present. They were aware of what was going on. No protest was made whatsoever and Mr. Dokmanovic was transported here. The Croatian authorities were in a position, had they wished to, to have stopped the aeroplane from taking off. It was a civilian airport on Croatian territory. I do not think there is any merit in the fact that Croatia has protested this. In fact, the arrests did occur on Croatian territory. Mr. Fila has also said that another option for the Tribunal was to have requested the extradition of Mr. Dokmanovic, since he is not a citizen of the FRY. The Office of the Prosecutor has no way of knowing where he has citizenship. He is a refugee in Serbia, coming from the area of Eastern Slavonija, Baranja, Western Srem. Mr. Knezevic is in the exact same circumstances, but according to Mr. Fila's written submissions, he is a citizen of the FRY. Any enquiries we would have made as to citizenship would obviously have tipped off the authorities as to what we were doing. The fact is, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is obligated to turn over the Tribunal anyone, regardless of whether they are a FRY citizen or not. Rule 58 states: "The obligations laid down in Article 29 of the statute shall prevail over any legal impediment to the surrender or transfer of the accused, or of a witness to the Tribunal which may exist under the national law or extradition treaties of the State concerned." It does not get any clearer than that. Yugoslavia has failed to co-operate with this Tribunal. The three co-defendants of Mr. Dokmanovic are still there, they have not turned them over. In the case of one of them, Veselin Sljivancanin, he is still a Colonel in the Yugoslav army. He is assigned to the Belgrade Military Academy. He is an indicted war criminal training officer cadets two kilometres from Slobodan Milosevic's house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Do you know what his citizenship is?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: He is Montenegran, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: I heard Mr. Dokmanovic testify at least that there was no citizenship, that he was a Yugoslav and that he did not -- that he did not consider that the republics did not have citizenship, but set that aside for a moment. Okay, so the others have not been turned over. One is a Montenegran -- what about the others?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The other two are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Serbs from the Federal --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: From Serbia proper, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: But the position of the Prosecutor is that this is just a technicality; that if a warrant had been directed to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, they would have reacted in the same way. They would not have turned over Mr. Dokmanovic. The only reason Drajan Erdemovic was turned over is the fact that he was an ethnic Croat. He was not a Serb, and I would contend that that is the true basis of whether the Federal Republic is cooperating, and it has nothing to do with where someone is holding citizenship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Does it make a difference? Is the Prosecutor required to first go to a state and then wait a certain period of time for the state not to execute an arrest warrant and then decide on an alternative way of accomplishing the arrest?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I do not believe we are, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If you have the power, you have the power. If you have the authority, rather, you have the authority, it seems to me. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Do we really need to go as far as the Machain case and Eichman? The Machain, Supreme Court case 1992, basically says they are not concerned with how a person gets to the court, with a very strong dissent, but unless we find that Mr. Dokmanovic was kidnapped by State authorities or perhaps by Prosecution authorities, then we need not go that far. This is an International Tribunal not bound by rules of any State, it seems to me, or decisions of any State and should look for the highest international standards, whether or not that is the highest international standard I suppose would be open to debate, but do we even need to go that far in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I would agree, your Honour, that the facts in this case are not nearly as egregious as they were in the Machain case. In that situation, as you said, it was an abduction, as it was in Eichman. A case that we had cited in one of our submissions though, I believe, is much more on point. This is regarding Hartnet, which is a Canadian case which I think is much more similar. This is paragraph 11 on page 6 of the Prosecution response of 14th August 1997. In this case, an American was invited across the Canadian border to testify in front of the Ontario Securities Commission in Toronto. Once he crossed the border, he was actually placed under arrest and his contention was that his invitation to testify was merely a ruse to get him across the border. The court upheld that and said this was appropriate. I think that situation is probably the closest of any of the cases that we have cited and I would agree that at this point in time you need not go as far as Machain, and enquire into abductions. This was not that type of situation. Clearly we used trickery, it was a ruse. It was the intention of the Prosecutor from day one to arrest Mr. Dokmanovic. From the moment Mr. Curtis got in contact with him, this was exactly what we wanted to accomplish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about that. Let me put it this way. Since the Prosecution either arrested Mr. Dokmanovic or, at the very least, participated jointly in the arrest, if the Prosecutor can be analogised to a State, if a State were to lure an individual into a jurisdiction through trickery or through some ruse, and then execute an arrest warrant, we do not go so far as to go through all of these procedures first, then would that violate the accused's rights, if you understand what I mean? Does it make a difference whether there is State involvement in the luring of an individual; for example, if the -- I cannot state it any better.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I follow what you are saying. I think that it is going to be appropriate whether State authorities are involved or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Do you know what the State of the law is in the United States as to trickery, setting aside Machain?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I believe that it would be upheld. I believe if the courts in the United States have gone so far as to uphold abductions, again they would not see using trickery as being as egregious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: There is one case - - let us set it aside. Okay, go ahead. You say that if the State was involved, what would be the effect of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I believe it would have no effect whether it was State or private individuals. In fact, I am aware in the United States there are often these cases, which I am sure you are familiar with from your work there, of what are called bounty hunters, people who go out and actually make arrests on people who have fled from their bail obligations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is because the individuals, though usually in the statement of bail, relinquish certain rights that they might otherwise have; is that not so or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is correct, but in any event, my point I was trying to make, I was not going down that road, these are arrests that occur by private individuals. I do not think it would be any different if those arrests were to occur by State authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. And the safe conduct, have you addressed that issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I have not. Your Honour, I think the testimony is very clear on this. Mr. Dokmanovic was not given any type of guarantee of safe conduct. I think that based on the circumstances, one could have been implied. I do not doubt for a second that he believed that he had some type of right of passage into the area and out again, but the point is nothing was explicitly stated in this regard. He did not ask a specific question about it. Nothing was told to him. Mr. Curtis has testified to that effect, Mr. Hryshchyshyn has testified to that effect and Witness A, the interpreter, has testified to that effect. Mr. Hryshchyshyn had indicated that Mr. Dokmanovic had told him that he was concerned about the Croatian authorities so what he had offered was to put him in a UN vehicle which would allow him to pass a checkpoint. This is not a guarantee of safe passage. In any event, even had he been given some type of guarantee of safe passage, it is our position that he still could have been arrested and that it would have been appropriate to arrest him. There was a valid order of this court, there was nothing that anyone from the Office of the Prosecutor could have said or that UNTAES could have said. They would have disregarded this order, avoided it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: That is very troublesome to me, because this Tribunal, the Trial Chamber, has been asked to give a safe conduct to one witness who appeared, and we did, and we have given it to many other witnesses who appeared in trials. When we do it, we are very precise about the language that is used, and that is a point you have not really pointed to, but you do not just give safe conduct, you point out from whom the person is protected in a safe conduct. The ones that we issue, we would say that the Prosecution may not detain a person for any acts that they committed before while they are present in The Hague. If you are telling me that that piece of paper means nothing?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No, your Honour, not at all. What I am saying is that is an order of this court and that is the reason that we as the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, that is very rude.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is the reason that we as the Prosecutor or they as the Defence file a motion requesting safe conduct from the court. That is an order from the court, just as this warrant for the arrest was. My point is that we as the Office of the Prosecutor have no authority on our own to overrule an order of this court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Do you even have an authority to grant safe conduct? If, for example, this Tribunal were to issue -- the arrest warrant, for example, is an outstanding arrest warrant, does the Prosecution have authority to give an individual the right -- freedom from arrest when this court has executed an arrest warrant?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No, we do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Why do you say it does not make any difference, if you did give safe conduct, because you would not have to honour it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: That is exactly it. We do not have the authority to give safe conduct. Even if we had as part of a ruse, it was not binding. It did not come up. Mr. Dokmanovic did not request any specific safe conduct or exemption from arrest by anyone. He expressed concern about the Croatian authorities, that was addressed. The first anyone heard of safe conduct was when motions were filed by Mr. Fila to that effect, saying he had received some grant of safe conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The audio and the transcript has been filed under seal. You have not admitted it or is that not under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The audio tapes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: The audio and the transcript of it. We had asked at a Status Conference that they be filed. Of course, we have resolved the video issue, but the transcript itself reflects what went on during the arrest, that the accused was read his rights et cetera, and the Prosecution has taken the position that there has been no violation of rights. Has that been made a part of the record for this hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: I am not sure if it has or not, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: No, it has not. You have not offered it as an exhibit, and I gather that is not under seal, the audio and the transcript. Is that so? The reason is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: The Defence has received a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: It should be made part of the record. When we make the decision, it seems to me we should be able to refer to what was told Mr. Dokmanovic, how he was informed of his rights, and unless we either have it as an exhibit in this proceeding or it is otherwise on record and it is not sealed, then that cannot be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: We would have no objection certainly to the portion of the tape that deals with his advisory of rights being made public. My only concern is that Mr. Dokmanovic makes a rather lengthy statement during the course of the aeroplane trip back which is also contained on the audio trip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Can you meet with Mr. Fila and perhaps the two of you can agree as to the portion that should be admitted and make that a part of the record, so it would be Prosecution exhibit whatever it may be, so that we may make use of it when we draft our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I do not think that is a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If there is any problem with that attempting to reach an agreement, then the Trial Chamber will assist you. That will then come in as a Prosecution exhibit. Is there any objection to that procedure, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: On the contrary, I agree fully that the parts that you considered confidential in the video should be considered confidential in the audio tape. I think you made a decision that only in courtroom we can see the video and that part that can be seen should not be released in the public. I think that this is the decision that you made and this is the right decision. We cannot have two decisions contradicting each other. I think Mr. Clint Williamson will agree with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: If the Chamber is to make a decision that Mr. Dokmanovic was properly advised of his rights, et cetera, no one has testified to it, we need something in a conclusory way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Certainly, your Honour, no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Very good. Well then, you meet with Mr. Fila and see if agreement can be reached, and that would then be admitted as a Prosecution exhibit. Do you have anything else to say in a few moments, Mr. Williamson?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: No, your Honour. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a clarification, both sides have expressed their views, I would just like to clarify one thing as to the nationality or citizenship of persons that you mention. Mr. Sljivancanin is a citizen of Republic of Serbia because he comes from Montenegra, whereas Mr. Mrksic and Mr. Radic are not citizens of Serbia, they are not Serbs, they live in Bosnia. So you do not have the correct information. Mr. Sljivancanin is protected by our constitution according to our position on this. My personal opinion has no importance. The position of the State is important here and the State of Yugoslavia believes that they cannot extradite their own citizens. So I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Is there anything else, Mr. Williamson?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILLIAMSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just add this very quickly, that in relation to Mr. Sljivancanin, I think that if this was a matter of a technicality of him not being extradited -- that the only bar to him coming to the Tribunal is the fact that he is a Yugoslav citizen, he would still not be in command of the Military Academy training their officer cadets. I think that goes much more to what the intent is of the Federal Republic as opposed to what his citizenship is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MCDONALD
utterances.text: Let us not argue so many things that are outside of the record. It is getting late and so if there is nothing else from the parties and all of the exhibits are in except for this one regarding advising the accused of his rights, then we will adjourn, a decision will be entered with respect to the Defence's motion as to the legality of the arrest in due course. We stand adjourned. (5.50 pm) (Court adjourned) 20 21 22 23 24 25
